files.text:
Queensland · 1893

A reef in thirteen stones

William Saville-Kent spent the years around 1890 as Commissioner of Fisheries for Queensland, and much of that time on the reef itself: on the flats at low spring tides, when the corals stand clear of the water for an hour, and at his tanks, where he kept living colonies long enough to draw them with their polyps out. Dead coral is white and every collector knew it. What he wanted to show in London was the colour, which fades within hours of a coral leaving the sea, so he painted them alive, in watercolour, and wrote under each plate del. et pinx. ad nat.: drawn and painted from nature.

The book came out in 1893, a heavy quarto with photographs of the reef flats and sixteen plates in colour. The colour plates were not photographs and not hand-painted. They were chromolithographs, printed by Riddle & Couchman of London from his watercolours, one colour at a time, each colour from its own slab of limestone.

A lithographic stone is fine Bavarian limestone, ground flat and then grained with sand until it has a tooth like paper. The printer's artist traced the outline of the whole picture, the key, and offset a print of it in red chalk onto each of the other stones as a guide. Then, stone by stone, he drew only what would take one ink: on the yellow stone every part of the plate where yellow lies, in greasy crayon, pressing harder where it should be stronger. The grain breaks the crayon into specks, which is why every colour here, seen close, is a scatter of dots on the paper, and why one ink laid over another makes a third without ever blending.

To print, the stone was damped, rolled up with ink that would stick only to the grease, and the sheet laid on it against the register pins. The bed was cranked under a fixed scraper, so the impression travelled down the sheet as a line. The whole edition went through on one stone and was left to dry before the next stone went on the press, so a printer could hold up a sheet halfway through and see a reef that was only yellow and pink, with no edges yet and no shadow. The greens came from blue over yellow, the deep red-browns of the brain corals from several passes on top of each other, and the drawing only became sharp with the darkest stone, the last one, which sat crisp on everything beneath it.

Nothing on a stone could be corrected once the edition was under way, and every stone had to fall on the same pins as the last, to within a hair, or each coral would be edged with a thin line of the wrong colour. Look closely at any plate of the period and you can find where they missed. Here they mostly did not. A coral in a museum drawer is a white skeleton; this was the reef as Saville-Kent saw it at low water, with the animals out, and for most people in England it was the first colour they had seen of a living reef.

# coral-reef The Great Barrier Reef as William Saville-Kent showed it to London in 1893: Chromo V, "Great Barrier Reef Corals", from *The Great Barrier Reef of Australia*, printed in front of you as you scroll, stone by stone, the way Riddle & Couchman printed it. The sheet starts as bare plate paper. The key goes through the press first: the drawing in the plate's brown-crimson, the outlines and meanders of the corals, the frame line and the lettering. Then one stone per ink, lightest first: chrome yellow, buff, an olive yellow and an ochre, the blue-green, a grey olive and a sage, the vermilion, and four crimson-browns that build the brain corals and the dark reef bank, darkest last. Each stone prints along the scraper's line as the press bed travels, so the new colour arrives as a slightly uneven front moving down the sheet; just behind it the oily ink is a shade deeper with a faint gloss, and then it sets matte. Anything a stone has not yet printed is simply not there. The last frame is the scan of the plate, pixel for pixel. Scroll back and it un-prints. ```html
``` Or `import { coralReef } from './coral-reef.js'` and call `coralReef(section, { src, mode, runway, webgl })`. It returns `destroy()`, which removes the canvas, listeners, observers and GL resources. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---------------|----------|----------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The plate's JSON: size, paper field, the stones (name, ink, scale, weight), the run, file names. Beside it: `reef.webp` (the plate), `reef-g0.webp` ... `reef-g12.webp` (one stone each, greyscale coverage) and `reef-time.webp` (lossless, half size: the scraper's line and drying). | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned stage on a runway. `static`: the finished plate as an image. | | `data-runway` | `runway` | `560` | Section height in svh. The stage is pinned for `runway - 100` svh, about 35 svh per stone. | | `data-webgl` | `webgl` | `on` | `off` leaves the finished plate as an image. | The run is `run: [-0.07, 0.95]` of the runway, shared among the stones by `weight` (the key gets 1.4, the rest 1). Progress starts a little below zero while the section's top is still coming up the screen, so the key is printed as the sheet arrives and the pinned stage opens on a confident drawing rather than a blank sheet. Inside each stone's slice the scraper crosses the sheet in the first 74%, then the sheet comes off the press and the ink sets before the next stone goes on. No two stones are ever on the press at once, as in the shop: the whole edition went through one stone before the next. Events (bubbling, for sound later): `coral-reef:stone` with `detail: { index, name }` as each stone goes on the press while scrolling forward, and `coral-reef:done` after the last impression. ## The real thing Read: George Richmond's *Grammar of Lithography* (1880) on chromolithographic practice; Michael Twyman, *A History of Chromolithography* (British Library, 2013); Peter Marzio, *The Democratic Art* (1979); and the plate itself at full resolution. - **The artwork.** Saville-Kent, Commissioner of Fisheries for Queensland from 1889, painted living corals in watercolour, on the reef flats at low spring tides and in tanks, because their colour goes within hours of leaving the water: "W. Saville-Kent, del. et pinx. ad nat." is printed under the plate. The printer, "Riddle & Couchman, Imp. London, S.E.", is printed on the other side. - **One stone per colour.** The printer's artist draws a key (the outline) and offsets impressions of it onto every other stone as a non-printing guide. On each grained stone he draws, in greasy crayon, only what takes that ink, pressing harder where it should be stronger. The grain breaks the crayon into specks: at 100% every colour on this plate is a scatter of dots, and greens are often a blue-green over a yellow, each grain still visible. That is exactly what the unmixing finds (below). - **The press.** The stone is damped and rolled up with ink, the damp sheet is laid on it against the register pins, and the bed is cranked under a fixed scraper, so the impression is made along a line that travels across the sheet. Here the line runs down the sheet, slightly bowed and a touch uneven where the damp sheet cockles, with a faint damp band at the line itself. Fresh litho ink is oily: a little deeper and glossy, then matte as it sets (thin films first, heavy deposits last). - **Order.** Light to dark, the darkest stone last so that it sits crisp on top. The key is printed first here, as a full drawing in the plate's line colour. That is a reconstruction: printers did print the key early on some plates, and it gives the opening a confident drawing, but the order on this plate is not documented. Simplified: there are thirteen passes; the real plate may have used more stones (some inks here are probably two stones that share a colour). The key is split from the dark inks by where they form line work, not from a real key impression. The stone itself, the roller and the tympan are not shown: you watch the sheet as if the press were glass, the way a printer looked at progressive proofs. No misregistration is added (this edition is well registered). ## How it works **Offline** (Python, numpy/scipy/scikit-learn/scikit-image; scripts in the builder's scratch folder, not in the component). All of it in linear-light optical density. 1. *The sheet.* The Internet Archive JP2 (5751x7581) cropped to the sheet inside the binding. 2. *The paper.* A robust cubic fit, per channel, to the bare paper between the specimens: the sheet's own toning, which the shader evaluates from ten coefficients. `D = -ln(O / paper)`. 3. *The inks.* Sparse dictionary learning on 250,000 pixels: each pixel is explained by at most two inks with non-negative coverage (closed-form two-ink least squares over every pair), inks re-fitted from the coverages, 14 rounds, from a k-means start. Twelve inks come out, sorted light to dark. Every pixel of the 2400px master is then coded against them. 4. *The key.* A ridge filter (Sato, sigma 1-2.6 px) on the dark inks' density finds the line work; long components are kept, plus everything in the margins (the lettering). That share of the dark inks is refitted as one ink, the key, and taken out of the dark stones. 5. *Export.* Coverage resampled by area to 1800px wide, scaled per stone, one greyscale WebP each. The time map: the scraper's line (down the sheet, bowed, cockle fBm) and a drying map. A Python copy of the shader proves the end frame equals the shipped plate (max error 0.5/255, float precision). **In the browser.** One quad, one fragment shader (WebGL2; WebGL1 without mipmaps). The thirteen greyscale stones are packed three to a texture once, at load. Per pixel: `D_O` from the plate and the paper field; each stone's density `a_k d_k`; the residual `R = D_O - sum(a_k d_k)` (what the inks do not explain: paper texture, scan noise). The shown density is `R·eps/(S+eps) + sum c_k (a_k d_k (1 + wet) + R·lum(a_k d_k)/(S+eps))`, where `c_k` is whether the scraper's line has passed this pixel for stone `k` and `S` is the total ink. The residual is shared between the bare paper and the stones in proportion to the ink each lays, so when every stone has printed `D = D_O` and the pixel is the plate, exactly, and before that nothing of an unprinted stone shows. The colour is `paper · exp(-D)`. - Scroll is followed by a critically damped spring (quicker going back). Nothing runs while the scroll is still, off screen (IntersectionObserver) or in a hidden tab. DPR capped at 2. - The canvas draws the sheet's edge and a tight shadow on the page itself. No vignette. - No camera: the whole plate stays in view and prints as a whole. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---------------|-----------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the page around the sheet (read from the section's background) | | `--cr-gutter` | `var(--gutter)` | side padding of the stage (the demo uses 8px on phones so the plate fills the width) | | `--cr-runway` | set by the script | section height in scroll mode | The sheet keeps the plate's own paper. ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS, without WebGL, or with `data-webgl="off"`, the finished plate is an ``. The canvas is `aria-hidden`; the art is ornament (`alt=""`), credits in `assets/credits.json`. - Reduced motion: no runway, no canvas, the finished plate. If the setting changes mid-visit it settles on the finished plate. - Nothing is interactive, so a swipe always scrolls. No UI and no caption on the page. ## Cost - Assets about 5.9 MB: the plate 1.1 MB, thirteen stones 4.4 MB, time map 0.25 MB, JSON 3 KB. - At load, the stones are read back once (thirteen 1800x2658 canvases) and packed into five RGBA textures: about 200 ms on a laptop and 94 MB of texture with mips. - One full-screen quad, ten texture reads and two short loops over thirteen stones per pixel, only while the scroll spring is moving. ## Credits William Saville-Kent, *Great Barrier Reef Corals* (Chromo V), chromolithograph printed by Riddle & Couchman, London, in *The Great Barrier Reef of Australia*, 1893. Smithsonian Libraries copy via the Internet Archive and the Biodiversity Heritage Library. Public domain. The separation into stones, the key and the time map are ours. No third-party code.
